blocks.c: It was small. It was brass.
It was not our key. Ours is in the desk drawer on Floor Zero, signed for, logged, in the inventory, with a receipt.
This one had a paper tag, and the tag was not paper I recognised, and the handwriting was not Wen's block capitals or Mrs. Dalisay's small clear hand or the clerk's neat old-fashioned clerking.
I photographed it. I logged it. I did not touch it. I took the photograph down to minus eleven and put it on the counter and asked the only question that mattered.

The clerk looked at the photograph for a long time. Long enough that I understood the answer before it spoke, and long enough for me to work out that I had been assuming, for four months, that a building with a lease was a building that was unique, and that this was an assumption I had never once written down.
"Mr. Oduya," it said. "How many premises do you imagine were leased in 1874?"
I went back up. I did the 05:00 walk: thirty-one landings, two basements, four risers, the roof. I logged the ficus, which is dying again, and the door closer on 22, which will outlive us all.
Then I sat down in the facilities office at ten to six with a black book and a pen and wrote the only entry that has ever frightened me while I was writing it.
05:52. Key found taped under extinguisher bracket, B2. Not ours. Tag reads HENDRY STREET. Photographed, logged, left in place.
Recommendation: two caretakers required per premises. We have two. They have none.
I am going to Hendry Street.
